rhetorical

rih-TOR-ih-kul -- shares a root with 'rhetoric,' the art of persuasive speaking. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Rhetorical is asked purely for effect or to make a point, not expecting or requiring an actual answer.

When she asked, "Do I look like I have time for this?" it was clearly a rhetorical question with no answer expected.

Example

A teacher looks at a classroom full of half-finished homework and asks the rhetorical question, "Does anyone actually read the instructions anymore?" -- not pausing for a single student to respond.

That question asked purely to make a point, not to gather information, is exactly what rhetorical describes. Unlike a genuine question, a rhetorical one already assumes its own answer.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

figurative: Figurative language makes a point through imagery or exaggeration instead of literal fact -- 'my feet are blocks of ice.' A rhetorical question works differently: its words are usually meant literally; what makes it rhetorical is that no answer is expected.

leading: A leading question nudges the listener toward a particular answer -- 'You saw him there, didn't you?' -- and it still expects a reply. A rhetorical question expects no reply at all: its answer is assumed, and the asking itself makes the point.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

literal: meant exactly as stated, without exaggeration

sincere: genuinely seeking a true answer

Where it sits · from single remark to whole speaking style — pointed → rhetorical → oratorical

pointed vs. rhetorical: Pointed is broader than rhetorical -- a pointed remark is simply direct and aimed at making a point, while rhetorical specifically describes a question asked for effect, with no answer expected.

oratorical vs. rhetorical: Oratorical can feel grander than rhetorical: rhetorical describes one particular kind of question, while oratorical describes an entire formal, persuasive style of public speaking.

Put it together

Put it together: Rhetorical traces to Greek rhetor, 'a public speaker,' whose art was rhetoric -- persuasive speaking. A rhetorical question is a speaker's tool, asked purely for effect rather than to get an answer.
